title: New Profit-Sharing Ratio and the Sacrificing Ratio
summary: How to work out the new ratio when a partner is admitted and how to find each old partner's sacrifice, with fraction examples.

p: When a new partner is admitted, the partners must agree the new profit-sharing ratio. It depends on the share the new partner is to receive, whether the old partners give up equal or unequal parts, and any special agreement about future profits.

sections.h: Example 1: the new partner takes from the old partners in the old ratio
p: A and B share profits 3 : 2. C is admitted and takes 1/5 of the profit. The remaining 4/5 is shared between A and B in 3 : 2.

Sacrifice = old share – new share. A: 3/5 – 12/25 = 15/25 – 12/25 = 3/25. B: 2/5 – 8/25 = 10/25 – 8/25 = 2/25. Sacrificing ratio A : B = 3 : 2. (When the new partner takes from the old partners in their old ratio, the sacrificing ratio is the same as the old ratio.)

sections.h: Example 2: the new ratio is given
p: A and B share 3 : 2. The new ratio of A : B : C is 5 : 3 : 2. Write the shares over 10: old A 6/10, B 4/10; new A 5/10, B 3/10, C 2/10. Sacrifice: A = 6/10 – 5/10 = 1/10; B = 4/10 – 3/10 = 1/10. So the sacrificing ratio is 1 : 1, and C's goodwill would be shared equally by A and B.

sections.h: Example 3: one partner gives up the whole share
p: A and B share equally. C takes 1/4, all from A. New: A = 1/2 – 1/4 = 1/4, B = 1/2, C = 1/4. New ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Sacrifice: A 1/4, B nothing. A receives all of C's goodwill.
The gaining ratio is used when a partner retires or dies and the continuing partners gain: gaining ratio = new ratio – old ratio. You will meet it in later work.

1. Write the old shares as fractions with a common denominator. 2. Write the new shares the same way. 3. Subtract new from old for each old partner. 4. Express the answers as a ratio. 5. Check that the sacrifices add up to the new partner's share.

title: Non-Profit Organisations and the Receipts and Payments Account
summary: Why clubs and societies do not prepare trading accounts, and the meaning, features and format of the receipts and payments account.

sections.h: Organisations that do not aim at profit
p: Schools, clubs, associations, churches and mosques are non-profit organisations. They exist to serve members or the public, not to make a profit. So they do not prepare Trading and Profit and Loss Accounts. Instead they prepare a Receipts and Payments Account and an Income and Expenditure Account.
It is a summary of all the cash and bank transactions of the organisation for a period (usually a year). It is the cash book written as a summary.
It is prepared on a cash basis: it records the actual cash received and paid, whatever period it relates to.

Features: like a cash book, with cash and bank; includes both capital and revenue items; includes payments for the past or next year; does not separate recurring from non-recurring items; shows the opening and closing balances; does not show surplus or deficit; it only shows money movements.
Receipts go on the debit side; payments go on the credit side. The balance carried down is the closing cash and bank balance.

sections.h: Typical receipts and payments of a club
p: Receipts: members' subscriptions; entrance fees; donations; sale of old assets; interest; proceeds from social events or games. Payments: salaries and wages; rent and electricity; stationery; purchase of equipment or furniture; prizes; repairs; refreshments.

Capital receipts or payments change the assets or the fund of the club (sale or purchase of furniture, building fund donations, life membership fees). Revenue items are the normal day-to-day income and expenses (subscriptions, wages). The receipts and payments account shows both. The income and expenditure account (next unit) shows only revenue items.

title: The Income and Expenditure Account
summary: Preparing the income and expenditure account from receipts and payments: surplus or deficit, accrual adjustments and the differences between the two accounts.

p: The Income and Expenditure Account is like the Profit and Loss Account of a business. It finds the surplus (income more than expenditure) or the deficit (expenditure more than income) of a non-profit organisation for the period. It is prepared on an accrual basis: it records the income earned and the expenses incurred in the year, whether or not cash has been received or paid.

It records only revenue items: capital items are left out. It includes only items relating to the current year, adjusted for amounts accrued or prepaid. It includes depreciation. It does not show cash opening or closing balances. If Income is more than Expenditure the balance is a surplus; if Expenditure is more than Income it is a deficit.
Expenditure on the debit side; income on the credit side.

sections.h: Steps for converting to an income and expenditure account
p: 1. Start from the receipts and payments account. 2. Remove capital items (sale or purchase of assets, capital donations, legacies, building fund). 3. Adjust for accrued and prepaid income and expenses (add what is owing, remove what belongs to other years). 4. Add depreciation on assets. 5. Add up both sides; the balance is the surplus or deficit. 6. The surplus or deficit is added to or taken from the accumulated fund on the balance sheet.

Subscriptions for the year = cash received – arrears for last year received this year – subscriptions paid in advance for next year + arrears for this year not yet paid. Treat each item carefully: this rule shows the accrual idea.

title: Non-Profit Accounts: Worked Example and Solutions
summary: The ABC Club example in full, and the solution to both assignments.

p: Receipts: opening balance ₦10,000; subscriptions ₦50,000; donations ₦20,000; sale of old chairs ₦15,000. Payments: salaries ₦30,000; stationery ₦5,000; electricity ₦4,000; purchase of furniture ₦25,000. Closing balance = ?
Assume ₦20,000 of the donations is capital, and ₦5,000 of the subscriptions received relates to the previous year.

Income: subscriptions 50,000 – 5,000 = 45,000. (The donation of 20,000 is capital, so it is left out; the sale of chairs and the purchase of furniture are capital items, so they are left out.) Expenditure: salaries 30,000 + stationery 5,000 + electricity 4,000 = 39,000. Surplus = 45,000 – 39,000 = ₦6,000.
Assignment 1: opening ₦5,000; subscriptions ₦30,000; donations ₦10,000 = receipts 45,000. Payments: equipment 15,000; salaries 12,000; stationery 3,000 = 30,000. Closing balance = ₦15,000.

Assignment 2: all the ₦10,000 donations are capital, so they are left out. Subscriptions = 30,000 – 2,000 (last year) = 28,000. Expenditure: salaries 12,000 + stationery 3,000 + depreciation 1,000 = 16,000. The purchase of equipment is capital and is left out. Surplus = 28,000 – 16,000 = ₦12,000.

In the lesson note the balance sheet or fund is not shown. In real accounts, the surplus is added to the accumulated fund (the club's capital) and the equipment, furniture and cash are shown as assets in a balance sheet.

title: Single Entry and Incomplete Records
summary: What single entry is, why some traders use it, its features and limitations and how it compares with double entry.

p: Most established businesses keep full double-entry records, where every transaction has a debit and a credit. Small traders, however, may not know accounting or may not wish to pay an accountant, so they keep only part of the records. This is called single entry or incomplete records.

Typically such a trader keeps the cash and bank transactions and the personal accounts of debtors and creditors. The trader leaves out complete ledger accounts (capital, expenses, income), real and nominal accounts, and regular balancing.

The double-entry principle is not applied consistently. Often only personal accounts and cash and bank records exist. Real and nominal accounts (assets, liabilities, expenses and incomes) are not fully kept. A trial balance cannot be prepared. The final accounts (Trading and Profit and Loss) cannot be prepared directly without extra work.
Lack of accounting knowledge; small size of the business; wish to reduce the cost of keeping books; informal arrangements; little legal need for detailed reports.

Errors and fraud are not easy to discover. A reliable trial balance cannot be made. The true financial position is hard to see. It is not good enough for planning or decisions. It is not accepted for tax purposes or by auditors, banks and investors.

title: Statement of Affairs Method: Finding Profit from Capital
summary: How to find profit when only assets and liabilities are known, using the statement of affairs and the capital formula, with worked examples and solutions.

p: The statement of affairs lists the assets and liabilities of the trader at a date. The difference is the capital: Capital = Assets – Liabilities. If we find the capital at the start and at the end of the year, the change tells us how much profit was made, after allowing for drawings and any new capital put in.
Profit or loss = Closing capital – Opening capital + Drawings – Additional capital introduced.
Why? Closing capital = Opening capital + Profit + Additional capital – Drawings. Rearranging gives the formula. If the answer is negative, it is a loss.
Opening capital ₦100,000; closing capital ₦130,000; drawings ₦15,000; additional capital ₦5,000. Profit = 130,000 – 100,000 + 15,000 – 5,000 = ₦40,000.

Step 1: list the assets at the date (cash, bank, stock, debtors, furniture) with their values. Step 2: list the liabilities (creditors, loans, bank overdraft). Step 3: capital = total assets – total liabilities. Do this for the opening date and the closing date.
Evaluation question 5: opening 80,000; closing 120,000; drawings 10,000; additional capital 5,000. Profit = 120,000 – 80,000 + 10,000 – 5,000 = ₦45,000.
Assignment: opening 60,000; closing 85,000; drawings 12,000; additional capital 8,000. Profit = 85,000 – 60,000 + 12,000 – 8,000 = ₦29,000.
Items usually missing in single entry: complete ledger accounts; capital account; expense accounts (rent, wages); income accounts; asset accounts; the trial balance. (Any three.)

sections.h: Statement of affairs and balance sheet
p: They look alike (assets, liabilities, capital) but a balance sheet comes from double-entry records and balances because of the books, while a statement of affairs is an estimate made from lists and valuations, and the capital is the balancing figure.

title: Reconstructing the Missing Accounts
summary: How to rebuild total debtors, total creditors and cash records to find credit sales and credit purchases, with a worked example.

p: The second way to deal with incomplete records is to rebuild the missing accounts from the information we do have. The three most useful reconstructions are the cash and bank summary, the total debtors account and the total creditors account. The missing figure in each is found as the balancing figure.

It collects everything that changed the total owed by customers. Debit side: opening debtors; credit sales (the balancing figure if unknown). Credit side: cash and cheques received from debtors; discount allowed; bad debts written off; sales returns; closing debtors.
Credit side: opening creditors; credit purchases (the balancing figure). Debit side: cash paid to creditors; discount received; purchases returns; closing creditors.

Total sales = cash sales + credit sales (from the debtors account). Total purchases = cash purchases + credit purchases (from the creditors account). With these figures and the expenses from the cash book, a trading account and a profit and loss account can be prepared, and the balance sheet figures are taken from the statement of affairs.

List all receipts and payments from the cash book. The opening balance and the closing balance help to find any missing item (such as cash drawings or cash sales) as the balancing figure. Always check that total receipts equal total payments.
The lesson note only lists these accounts; the examples above are our own to show how the balancing figures work.

title: First Term Revision: Partnership, Non-Profit and Single Entry
summary: A checklist of the term's formulas and formats, with the answers to the main assignments in one place.

p: Appropriation account: net profit, interest on capital, salaries, interest on drawings (credit side), remaining profit in the ratio. Capital accounts: fixed and fluctuating. Current account: debit drawings and interest on drawings; credit interest on capital, salary and profit share. Admission of a partner: reasons; revaluation (old ratio); new ratio; sacrificing ratio; goodwill journals. Non-profit accounts: receipts and payments (cash basis); income and expenditure (accrual basis). Single entry: statement of affairs; reconstruct debtors and creditors.

Interest on capital = capital × rate. Remaining profit = net profit + interest on drawings – salaries – interest on capital. Sacrificing ratio = old share – new share. Profit (single entry) = closing capital – opening capital + drawings – additional capital. Surplus = income – expenditure.

Appropriation (C and D): interest 5,000 and 7,000; remaining 81,000; C 32,400, D 48,600. Capital account (C): closing balance 112,000. Current account B (Week 3): 20,600 credit. Current account B (Week 4): 19,000 credit. Admission: new ratio 12 : 8 : 5; sacrifice 3 : 2; journal Dr Bank 80,000, Cr C 60,000, Cr A 12,000, Cr B 8,000. Club R and P: ABC closing 31,000; assignment closing 15,000. I and E: ABC surplus 6,000; assignment surplus 12,000. Single entry: profits 45,000 and 29,000.
